questions.q: Why does Linux patch management split into different command sets instead of one unified command?
options: Patch commands are identical across all distributions with no real differences
Linux has no concept of package management at all
Every Linux distribution requires manually compiling updates from source code
Different distribution families use different package managers — APT for Debian/Ubuntu, YUM/DNF for the Red Hat family
questions.explain: Debian-family distributions use APT with .deb packages, while Red Hat-family distributions use YUM or DNF with .rpm packages.

options: Refreshes the local package index only — it does not install any updates
Removes all currently installed packages
Installs every available update immediately
Is identical in effect to apt upgrade
questions.explain: apt update refreshes the list of available package versions; apt upgrade is the separate step that actually installs newer versions.

questions.q: How does `yum update` (or `dnf upgrade`) differ from the apt workflow?
options: It only refreshes the package index and never installs anything
It refreshes repository metadata and installs available updates in a single command, instead of splitting that into two steps
It permanently disables all future updates once run
It is only available on Debian and Ubuntu systems
questions.explain: Unlike apt's two-step update/upgrade split, yum update and dnf upgrade combine refreshing metadata and installing updates into one command.

questions.q: What does `apt full-upgrade` (dist-upgrade) do differently from a plain `apt upgrade`?
options: It works exclusively on Red Hat-family systems
It has no behavioral difference from apt upgrade whatsoever
It is allowed to remove a package if that's what dependency resolution requires
It only checks for updates without installing anything
questions.explain: Plain apt upgrade never removes packages; full-upgrade/dist-upgrade can, when needed to satisfy dependencies.

questions.q: What is the real tradeoff of tools like unattended-upgrades or dnf-automatic?
options: They require a human to manually approve every single update before it installs
They eliminate all risk of a patch ever breaking a system
They close the patch gap automatically but remove the manual testing checkpoint, so the speed-vs-stability tension is automated rather than eliminated
They are only capable of installing non-security updates
questions.explain: Automatic patching removes delay but also removes the chance to test before deployment, which is why most real deployments scope it to security updates only.
